cards.title: Exponential repetition of two-player entangled games
cards.formal: Does every finite two-player, one-round game \(G\) with entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)<1\) admit a constant \(c_{G}>0\) such that \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq \exp(-c_{G}n)\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq1?\] The repetition uses the unchanged game and requires winning every coordinate. The 2016 paper proves convergence to zero at a polynomial rate; an August 2026 manuscript claims the exponential bound, with verification limits recorded below.

source_formulation.text: The results of Bavarian, Vidick and Yuen show that, while we do not know if the Quantum Parallel Repetition Conjecture holds for all games \(G, [\ldots ]\)

cards.why: Determines how reliably independent challenges amplify soundness against quantum players who may coordinate across all copies. The universal question isolates the effect of entanglement without adding auxiliary tests or restricting the form of the game.
cards.status_note: Claimed resolution found. Read the complete 2016 question and its polynomial-decay theorem, checked the author-version history, and read the August 2026 manuscript’s Chapter 6 Theorem 1.1 and Definitions 2.1–2.2. Its statement matches the full conjecture, but its proof and independent acceptance were not verified. Searches through 12 September 2026 do not justify either a confidently open label or a verified-resolved label. The old working summary’s “source-resolved” description applied only to convergence to zero.

progress.text: The full author paper announces polynomial decay for all two-player entangled games, resolving nonconvergence but leaving exponential decay open.
The conference introduction distinguishes the full exponential conjecture from amplification through game transformations.
The updated manuscript claims an exponential bound for every finite two-player game in the required tensor-product strategy model. Independent proof verification was not completed in this review.

sentences: Two quantum players must win every copy of a fixed game repeated independently by the referee.
They may use arbitrary finite-dimensional entanglement and joint local measurements across the copies.
The target is exponential decay whenever the original optimal value is below one.
The original paper establishes only polynomial decay, while game transformations give a different amplification guarantee.
An August 2026 manuscript claims the full exponential theorem, but this review has not independently verified its proof.

cards.definitions:
A game is specified by finite nonempty question sets \(X,Y\), finite nonempty answer sets \(A,B\), a probability distribution \(\mu\) on \(X\times Y\), and a winning predicate \(V:X\times Y\times A\times B\to\{0,1\}\). The referee samples \((x,y)\) from \(\mu\), sends \(x\) only to Alice and \(y\) only to Bob, and accepts their answers \(a,b\) exactly when \(V(x,y,a,b)=1\). The two questions may be correlated, and some pairs may have probability zero.

Before receiving their questions, the players may share any finite-dimensional bipartite quantum state \(\rho\) on \(\mathcal H_{A}\otimes\mathcal H_{B}\). On question \(x\), Alice applies a measurement \(\{E^{x}_{a}:a\in A\}\); on question \(y\), Bob applies \(\{F^{y}_{b}:b\in B\}\). Each measurement is a family of positive semidefinite operators summing to the identity. Their conditional answer probability is
\[\Pr[a,b\mid x,y]=\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\rho(E^{x}_{a}\otimes F^{y}_{b})\bigr).\]
They cannot communicate after receiving the questions. Shared randomness is permitted and can be incorporated into the shared state.

The entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)\) is the supremum of the winning probability over all such finite-dimensional states and local measurements. The dimensions have no fixed upper bound, and a strategy attaining the supremum need not exist. This is the finite-dimensional tensor-product model, not the possibly larger commuting-operator or general nonsignaling model. No efficiency restriction is placed on a strategy.

In \(G^{\otimes n}\), the referee samples \(n\) independent pairs from \(\mu\), sends the complete tuple of Alice's questions to Alice and the complete tuple of Bob's questions to Bob, and receives answer tuples in \(A^{n}\) and \(B^{n}\). Acceptance requires \(V(x_{i},y_{i},a_{i},b_{i})=1\) for every coordinate \(i\).

Each player may use one joint local measurement depending on their entire tuple. Their shared state and its dimension may depend on \(n\). Thus independent sampling by the referee does not force independent play. Product strategies give the lower bound \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\geq\omega^{*}(G)^{n}\); this is not the requested upper bound.

The constant \(c_{G}\) may depend on the entire fixed game, including its soundness gap \(1-\omega^{*}(G)\). It must be positive and independent of \(n\), the strategy and its dimension. No universal optimal exponent or algorithm for computing \(c_{G}\) is requested. A transformed game with added questions is a different game and cannot replace \(G\) in this statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal exponential upper bound in the stated strategy model, or exhibit one fixed finite game with value below one for which no positive \(c_{G}\) works. A sequence of different games with progressively slower exponential constants is not a counterexample. Polynomial decay, convergence to zero, exponential decay only for a special game family, or amplification after changing the game does not settle the conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The 2016 theorem settles a weaker historical question
context_blocks.text: Yuen proves \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})=O_{G}(n^{-1/4}\log n)\) for \(n\geq2\). Hence the repeated value cannot stay bounded away from zero. The surrounding text explicitly leaves exponential decay as the full conjecture; the previous working summary conflated these two targets.

context_blocks.title: Changing the game already enables exponential amplification
context_blocks.text: The source describes anchoring and fortification transformations that add auxiliary questions and give exponential decay for the resulting game while preserving quantum completeness. This supplies useful gap amplification but does not bound standard repetition of every original game.

context_blocks.title: A 2026 manuscript claims the exact missing result
context_blocks.text: Chapter 6, Theorem 1.1, claims a universal \(c>0\) with \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq\exp\!\left(-c\,\frac{\varepsilon^{13}}{\varepsilon+\ln(|A||B|)}\,n\right),\qquad\varepsilon=1-\omega^{*}(G)>0.\] Its definitions allow arbitrary finite-dimensional joint strategies and correlated question distributions for the unchanged game. If valid, this resolves the displayed conjecture; the exponent \(13\) is not claimed optimal.

context_blocks.title: Statement matching is separate from proof validation
context_blocks.text: This review checked the manuscript’s version date, theorem and model against the original conjecture. It did not independently verify the proof or establish an independently reviewed publication of this result. The card therefore records an uncertain claimed resolution rather than labeling the conjecture securely open or verified resolved.

cards.context:
Yuen proves \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})=O_{G}(n^{-1/4}\log n)\) for \(n\geq2\). Hence the repeated value cannot stay bounded away from zero. The surrounding text explicitly leaves exponential decay as the full conjecture; the previous working summary conflated these two targets.

The source describes anchoring and fortification transformations that add auxiliary questions and give exponential decay for the resulting game while preserving quantum completeness. This supplies useful gap amplification but does not bound standard repetition of every original game.

Chapter 6, Theorem 1.1, claims a universal \(c>0\) with \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq\exp\!\left(-c\,\frac{\varepsilon^{13}}{\varepsilon+\ln(|A||B|)}\,n\right),\qquad\varepsilon=1-\omega^{*}(G)>0.\] Its definitions allow arbitrary finite-dimensional joint strategies and correlated question distributions for the unchanged game. If valid, this resolves the displayed conjecture; the exponent \(13\) is not claimed optimal.

This review checked the manuscript’s version date, theorem and model against the original conjecture. It did not independently verify the proof or establish an independently reviewed publication of this result. The card therefore records an uncertain claimed resolution rather than labeling the conjecture securely open or verified resolved.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
